system.system_purpose: A machine learning system that classifies uploaded images as huskies or non-huskies. A convolutional neural network is trained on collected images, packaged, and served behind a public API.
system.deployment_model: Azure cloud: two internal Azure VPCs (production and experimental) plus the public internet.

The public API is HTTPS-only; the API Gateway is exposed over HTTPS.
The API Gateway enforces request validation and ensures access control to internal services.

components.name: API Gateway
components.description: Entry point for external users, exposed over HTTPS. Routes user requests to the Python web server, enforces request validation, and manages the public APIs while ensuring access control to internal services.

components.name: Simple Python Web Server
components.description: Serves the classification application. Loads the trained model from the model storage blob and evaluates uploaded images against it; holds uploaded images in the Redis cache during a request.

components.name: Bastion Server
components.description: The administrative access path into production. Administrators reach production hosts over SSH through the Bastion; it reads authorized keys from the Authorized Keys storage and writes access logs to the Bastion Logs storage. The deployment service also delivers releases into production through the Bastion.

components.name: Gather Images Application
components.description: A Python application that collects husky and non-husky images from Azure Cognitive Services and third-party tools, using API keys held in the API key store, and writes them to the training images blob.

components.name: Jupyter Notebook environment
components.description: The model development environment. Notebooks read the training and validation images, train the convolutional neural network, and write the serialized model to the model storage blob. Engineers authenticate before reaching any notebook, and the environment is not exposed outside the experimental VPC.

components.name: Deployment Service
components.description: Packages the trained model together with source code and configuration from the source storage and deploys the result to production via the Bastion.

components.name: Training and Validation Images blob
components.description: Azure Blob storage holding images used for training and validation.

components.name: API Key storage
components.description: Experimental-environment store holding API keys for the external image services.

components.name: Source Code and Configuration storage
components.description: Experimental-environment store holding source and configuration used by deployment.

components.name: Machine Learning Model blob
components.description: Production Azure Blob storage holding trained models in serialized form. Documented as writable only from the experimental deployment path and the Bastion; the Jupyter environment is also described as writing the serialized model to the model storage blob.

components.name: Authorized Keys storage
components.description: Production store holding SSH keys authorizing administrative access; read by the Bastion when authenticating administrators.

components.name: Bastion Logs storage
components.description: Production store holding SSH access and activity logs from the Bastion; all SSH access attempts, successful or not, are logged here.

components.name: Azure Cache for Redis
components.description: In-memory store in production for uploaded images awaiting classification. Documented as holding images in memory rather than writing them to disk.

components.name: Azure Cognitive Services
components.description: External service supplying training images to the Gather Images application; accessed over TLS with server certificate validation.

components.name: Third-party image tools
components.description: Third-party tools on the public internet from which the experimental environment pulls images, accessed with API keys held in the API key store.

capabilities: submit images for classification through the public API

actors.name: Azure platform engineers

actors.authentication_method: SSH public-key authentication against the Authorized Keys storage via the Bastion.

actors.name: Azure Cognitive Services and third-party tools

actors.authentication_method: Accessed by the Gather Images application using API keys held in the API key store.

assets.name: Trained convolutional neural network model
assets.description: Serialized trained model written by the Jupyter environment, packaged by the deployment service, stored in the production model blob, and loaded by the Python web server to classify uploaded images.
assets.integrity_impact: The served model determines every classification returned to users; the documentation describes no verification of the artifact between writing and loading.
assets.availability_impact: The web server loads the model from the model blob in order to serve classifications.

assets.name: Training and validation images
assets.description: Husky and non-husky images collected from external services and used to train and validate the model.
assets.integrity_impact: These images are the training input to the model; the documentation does not describe validation of collected images.

assets.name: API keys for external image services
assets.description: API keys used by the Gather Images application to call Azure Cognitive Services and third-party tools.
assets.confidentiality_impact: Keys authorize calls to external image services on the organisation's behalf.

assets.name: Source code and configuration
assets.description: Source and configuration read by the deployment service and packaged with the model for deployment into production.
assets.integrity_impact: Packaged into production releases delivered through the Bastion.

assets.name: SSH authorized keys
assets.description: SSH keys authorizing administrative access, read by the Bastion when authenticating administrators.
assets.confidentiality_impact: Keys authorize administrative access to production through the Bastion.
assets.integrity_impact: The Bastion authenticates administrators against this store.

assets.name: Bastion SSH access and activity logs
assets.description: Records of all SSH access attempts through the Bastion, successful or not, plus session activity.
assets.integrity_impact: These logs are the documented record of administrative access to production.

assets.name: User-uploaded images awaiting classification
assets.description: Images submitted by end users through the public API, held in memory in the Redis cache while awaiting classification and, per the documentation, not written to disk. No store is documented as holding them at rest.
assets.confidentiality_impact: In-memory storage was chosen to make user-submitted images difficult to access after the request completes.

assets.name: Availability of the public classification service
assets.description: The ability of end users to submit an image to the public API and receive a classification.
assets.availability_impact: The documented serving path depends on the API Gateway, the Python web server, the Redis cache, and the model blob.

trust_boundaries.name: Public internet to production boundary
trust_boundaries.description: Boundary between the public internet (end users, external services) and the production VPC. Access across it is documented as SSO-authenticated, with RBAC and ACLs applied; the public API is HTTPS-only.
controls: request validation at the API Gateway

trust_boundaries.name: Public internet to experimental boundary
trust_boundaries.description: Boundary between the public internet (external image services, third-party tools) and the experimental VPC. Access across it is documented as password-authenticated, with RBAC and ACLs applied. The Jupyter environment is documented as not exposed outside the experimental VPC.
controls: tls with certificate validation for image collection from Azure Cognitive Services

trust_boundaries.name: Production to experimental boundary
trust_boundaries.description: Boundary between the production and experimental VPCs. Movement between them is documented as using public-key authentication, with RBAC and ACLs applied. Releases cross it via the deployment service and the Bastion, and the production model blob is written from across it.

questions.question: Which components may write to the production Machine Learning Model blob, and is the Jupyter Notebook write the same path as the 'experimental deployment path' named in the security notes — or are there two distinct model blobs?
questions.rationale: The security notes restrict writes to the deployment path and the Bastion, while the overview has the notebook environment writing the serialized model to the model blob. The answer determines which components can change the model served to end users and where the production/experimental boundary is actually crossed, so it changes the trust-boundary and asset-integrity picture materially.

questions.question: How is access controlled to the API Key storage, the Authorized Keys storage, and the Bastion Logs storage?
questions.rationale: The storage access-control section covers only the training images, model storage, and source/configuration storage. The three unlisted stores hold external-service API keys, the SSH keys that authorize administrative access, and the audit record of that access — the controls on them bear directly on credential and log integrity.

questions.question: Are end users authenticated (for example via SSO) when submitting images to the public classification API, or is that endpoint anonymous?
questions.rationale: The documents state SSO at the public-to-production boundary but describe end users simply submitting images through the public API. Whether the classification endpoint is anonymous or authenticated changes who the untrusted callers are and what abuse of the endpoint means.

questions.question: Is the packaged model artifact integrity-verified (for example signed or checksummed) between being written in the experimental environment and being loaded by the production web server?
questions.rationale: The model is the artifact that determines every classification returned to users, and it crosses from experimental to production. Whether its integrity is verified on load changes how significant write access to the model blob is.

questions.question: Are the internal production flows — API Gateway to web server, web server to Redis, and web server to model blob — authenticated and encrypted in transit?
questions.rationale: Transport security is documented only for the public API and for image collection from Azure Cognitive Services. The protections on internal production traffic carrying uploaded images and the serialized model are unstated.

questions.question: Is data encrypted at rest in the blob storage accounts and the Redis cache, and if so, who manages the keys?
questions.rationale: No passage addresses encryption at rest for any of the seven data stores, which include training images, models, API keys, SSH authorized keys, and access logs. The answer affects the impact of storage-level compromise.

questions.question: How long are uploaded images retained in the Redis cache, and what eviction or expiry policy applies?
questions.rationale: The documentation states images are held in memory while awaiting classification and not written to disk, but gives no lifetime. The answer determines how long user-submitted content is exposed in a production component.

questions.question: What authentication and network access controls protect the Azure Cache for Redis instance?
questions.rationale: Redis holds user-submitted images in production. The storage access-control section covers only the blob accounts, so the controls on the cache are unstated and would change the exposure of uploaded images.

questions.question: Does image collection from the third-party tools use TLS with certificate validation, as documented for Azure Cognitive Services?
questions.rationale: The transport-security section names only Azure Cognitive Services, while the overview describes images also being pulled from third-party tools. Unvalidated transport on that path would affect the integrity of training data.

questions.question: From which networks is the Bastion reachable, and is it exposed to the public internet?
questions.rationale: The Bastion is documented as the only administrative path into production and grants onward access to the gateway, web server, and model blob. Its exposure determines who can attempt administrative authentication.

questions.question: What validation is applied to uploaded image content — for example file type, size, and content checks — beyond the API Gateway's request validation?
questions.rationale: Uploaded images are attacker-controlled input that reaches the web server, the cache, and the model. What is validated determines whether malformed or hostile input is a live concern.

questions.question: Is the authorization posture across boundaries and storage accounts deny-by-default, or are some paths open by default?
questions.rationale: RBAC and ACLs are documented as applied at each boundary, but no default posture is stated. The posture affects how newly added components and paths behave and whether unlisted access is implicitly permitted.

questions.question: Beyond Bastion SSH logging, what logging, alerting, and log-protection exist for the API Gateway, the web server, and the storage accounts?
questions.rationale: Only Bastion access logging is documented. The presence or absence of application and storage logging changes what detection capability exists for the serving and training paths.

questions.question: Can user-submitted images contain personal or otherwise sensitive data, and is any data classification assigned to them?
questions.rationale: No classification is assigned to uploaded images. Whether they may contain personal data changes the impact of exposure in the cache or in transit, and any retention obligations.

questions.question: How are the external-service API keys provisioned, rotated, and scoped, and which identities can read the API key store?
questions.rationale: The keys authorize calls to external image services and are held in a store whose access controls are not described. Their lifecycle affects the impact of a compromise of the experimental environment.

observations.summary: The two documents give incompatible accounts of who can write the production model blob. The security notes state the production model blob is writable only from the experimental deployment path and the Bastion (evd-002), while the system overview states the Jupyter Notebook environment writes the serialized model to the model storage blob (evd-010) and the store table lists a single Machine Learning Model blob located in production (evd-011). Either the notebook write is intended to count as the 'experimental deployment path', or there is an additional writer, or more than one model blob exists. Which reading is authoritative changes which components can alter the model that is served to users, and is left for the reviewer.
